I've been farming this land for fifty years. My body isn't what it was — at 76, my knees ache and I can't do the heavy work like I used to. My wife and I manage together, but we're only two people on 4.1 mu. My children went to the city years ago.

**Wheat (winter):** The wheat goes in as it always does, after the maize comes off. I'll use the improved variety the seed station has been selling — better yield than the old seeds I used to save. I put down rotary tillage after maize harvest to break up the stubble. Three irrigations: at jointing, heading, and grain fill. Well water costs money and time to pump, so I don't overdo it. Two pesticide passes — one herbicide early, one for aphids or rust if I see it. Fifteen kilograms of nitrogen per mu is enough; I learned the hard way that more just lodges the stems.

**Maize (summer):** After wheat harvest I go straight in with hybrid maize seeds, no-till. At my age I'm not ploughing twice in a year if I don't have to. Summer rains help, so I only irrigate twice unless it's a dry July. Maize doesn't need as much attention as cotton — two pesticide applications keeps the corn borer manageable.

**Cotton (1.6 mu):** Cotton is hard work — topping, picking by hand, bollworm pressure. But I know cotton, and it fetches decent money. I'll plough in spring before transplanting. Four irrigations, five pesticide applications — you can't slack on cotton pests or you lose the whole thing. My hands know this work even if they're slower now.
